title: Lady Poverty
hookLine: Francis spoke of poverty as a bride: freedom from owning

lines: HE HANDS BACK EVEN HIS CLOTHES.
cards: A young man stands before the bishop in Assisi, a hill town in Italy. His father, a cloth merchant, is furious: the son has been giving away money and goods the father counts as his.

So the son does something nobody there expects. He hands back the money, then takes off his very clothes and hands those back too. From now on, the early accounts have him say, he'll call only God his father.
The bishop wraps his own cloak around him. The young man is Francis; you met him back on day eight hundred fourteen. And he's about to fall in love with someone unexpected.

teach.b: Francis spoke about poverty the way a knight in an old love song speaks of his lady: poverty was his bride, and he courted her. One early allegory turns it into a story.
Francis and his brothers climb a mountain to find Lady Poverty, and bring her down to share a meal: a little bread and cold water.
When she asks to see their cloister, they lead her to a hilltop and show her the whole world.
This, they say, is our cloister. Why a bride, and not a burden? Because for Francis, poverty meant freedom.
Things own you back. A house wants guarding, money wants counting, a fine coat wants protecting from the rain.
He heard the Gospel words where Jesus sends out his disciples, "Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses," and tradition says he took them at face value.

He looked at Jesus himself: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Owning nothing left Francis's hands free: for lepers, for the poor, for praise.

Nothing in his story makes forced hunger holy. In the early accounts, Francis chooses to share the life of the poor and stand beside them, and gives away what comes to him. Christians take his example in different ways.
Franciscan friars and sisters still take vows of poverty. Others hear it as a question to carry: how much is enough, and what do my things ask of me?

how: Franciscan friars and sisters take a vow of poverty and hold possessions in common; lay Franciscans and other Christians inspired by Francis practice simplicity and giving in ordinary life.

o: Francis's name for poverty, loved like a bride
a saint who begged on the streets of Rome
a noblewoman who funded the first friars

p: the Son of man hath not where to lay his head

s: Francis's father gladly blessed him giving everything away
his father was furious; Francis handed back even his clothes before the bishop.
in the old allegory, the brothers show Lady Poverty the whole world as their cloister
this, they say, is our cloister.
Lady Poverty means being forced to go without
for Francis it was a free choice, to share the life of the poor.

games.q: you're Francis, before the bishop. your father demands back the money and goods he says are his. what do you do?
o: pay him back and go home quietly.
hand back the money and even the clothes you're wearing.
slip out of town before anyone notices.
games.why: he gives back everything, clothes included, and says he'll call only God his father. the bishop covers him with his own cloak.

practice: Walk through your home in your mind, a closet, a shelf, a drawer, and find one thing you don't need that someone else could use: not the thing you'd never miss, but one with a little pull to it.
Hold it in mind and notice the tug; that pull is what Francis wanted to be free of. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Lady Poverty. Francis's name for the life of owning nothing, loved like a bride because it set him free.

orig.note: Latin: Lady Poverty, the name early Franciscan writings give her.

carryVoice: Your line: free of things. What you own can own you back. Back tomorrow, same hill.
